body: THE GOOD NUMBER: PC Jeweller grew sales and profits fast, opened stores and traded at a fraction of Titan's P/E, so it looked like 'Titan at a discount'; it peaked ~Rs 600 (Jan 2018, pre-split). WHY IT LIED: inventory and export receivables (largely to the UAE) rose much faster than sales and CFO stayed weak or negative for years despite reported profits, funded by gold-metal loans and bank working capital. The reported profit depended on receivables that later proved hard to collect. In 2018 the promoter 'gifted' shares to family off-market, a buyback was announced and then withdrawn (-43% in a week); 2021-22 the company defaulted on ~Rs 3,400 cr of bank loans. CONTRAST WITH TITAN: Titan's negative-CFO years came from gold inventory in its own stores with single-digit debtor days and a clean group; PC Jeweller's came from export receivables to counterparties outside India plus governance events. Same flag, different content. TEST: inventory and receivable days by segment (domestic retail vs export); who owes the money; does the discount to the leader reflect worse economics. LESSON: 'cheap versus the leader' is often the market correctly pricing lower-quality earnings.

data.good_number: fast sales and profit growth, a 'cheap' P/E vs Titan, expanding store count, export business
data.test_that_catches_it: inventory + receivable days trend; CFO/PAT; who the export customers are; promoter share 'gifts'
data.why_misleading: inventory and export receivables (UAE) grew faster than sales; CFO weak or negative for years; profits were not turning into cash

title: Hidden trap: PC Jeweller's growth, profits and low P/E
